https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/movies.text: By David Rooney Plus Icon David Rooney Chief Film Critic DavidCRooney1 Follow Sign Up View All September 6, 2026 7:35am Share on Facebook Share on X Google Preferred Share to Flipboard Show additional share options Share on LinkedIn Share on Pinterest Share on Reddit Share on Tumblr Share on Whats App Send an Email Print the Article Post a Comment 'Possible Love' Courtesy of Netflix Share on Facebook Share on X Google Preferred Share to Flipboard Show additional share options Share on LinkedIn Share on Pinterest Share on Reddit Share on Tumblr Share on Whats App Send an Email Print the Article Post a Comment In his exquisitely layered seventh feature, Possible Love ( Ga-neung-han sa-rang ), Lee Chang-dong ’s humanistic observational skills remain at their peak, the acuity of his insights into emotional lives and social conditions unparalleled. More straightforward though no less affecting than the haunting ambiguities of his last film, Burning , the Korean director’s melancholic new work turns his customary slow-burn approach to the simmering tensions between two couples from different economic strata. A profound meditation on trauma, loss of dignity, yearning and class envy, this is a sad but beautiful chamber piece, fleshed out by a superlative ensemble. Related Stories TV 'Sweet Magnolias' Canceled at Netflix After Five Seasons Business Netflix Stock Falls After Wells Fargo Downgrade: "Engagement Trends Look Worrying to Us" The project was announced as part of a series of reinterpretations by international directors of Krzysztof Kieslowski’s landmark Dekalog , which was made for Polish television and inspired by the Ten Commandments. Unlike Asghar Farhadi’s Cannes lowlight, Parallel Tales , Lee’s film is a complete narrative departure from that source. It shares little beyond the commandment at the heart of Kieslowski’s tenth chapter, “Thou shalt not covet,” and a rejection of the moral imperative that religious framework might imply. Possible Love The Bottom Line Another stunner from one of the greats of contemporary world cinema. Venue : Venice Film Festival (Competition) Release date : Friday Oct. 23 Cast : Jeon Do-yeon, Sul Kyung-gu, Zo In-sung, Cho Yeo-jeong, Jung Seol Director : Lee Chang-dong Screenwriters : Lee Chang-dong, Oh Jung-mi Rated R, 2 hours 44 minutes Following its premiere run at the Venice, Toronto and New York film festivals, Possible Love — recently chosen as Korea ’s submission in the international Oscar category — will open Oct. 23 in limited theatrical release before streaming on Netflix from Nov. 6. The story concerns a blue-collar couple, Ho-seok (Sul Kyung-gu) and his wife Mi-ok (Jeon Do-yeon), still struggling to bounce back from the loss of his factory job two years earlier after a brutal government crackdown on striking employees. When they arrive at the funeral of his former work colleague, taciturn Ho-seok refuses to enter the building, sending his wife and their withdrawn 10-year-old son Cheol (Jung Seol) in alone while he waits in the car. Unlike her brooding, clearly depressed husband, who refused counseling after his job loss, Mi-ok is cheerful and easygoing. She strikes up a rapport with Ye-ji (Cho Yeo-jeong), a documentary filmmaker interviewing attendees at the reception for a project about workforce shrinkage as AI and corporate restructuring eliminate jobs. When Ho-seok does finally come inside, he turns belligerent with Mi-ok, making a scene as she reminds him of his promise to restrict his drinking to when he’s at home. After Mi-ok’s recent weight loss, her wedding ring has become loose. When it slips off and rolls under a car in the parking lot outside, handsome stranger Sang-woo (Zo In-sung) helps her find it using the headlights of his Porsche. He is soon revealed to be Ye-ji’s husband, a wealthy businessman who exudes the breezy confidence that usually comes with money and privilege. Lee and his Burning co-writer Oh Jung-mi resist what might have been the first instinct of many filmmakers by refusing to make Ye-ji and Sang-woo overly patronizing rich jerks. Both characters are more nuanced, even if there are inherent ethical questions raised by a well-heeled documentarian choosing to make a film about vanishing labor. It’s telling that after being granted permission to film Mi-ok at her job in a small paper manufacturing plant, Ye-ji decides that the work is too simple and repetitive to be of interest, instead preferring to focus on her subjects’ personal histories. In an amusing throwaway moment, Mi-ok furtively photographs Ye-ji’s stylish handbag and prices it online, later commenting that the filmmaker’s chic, expensive outfits are perhaps not an ideal choice when she’s trying to blend in and talk to disenfranchised union workers. Glancing observations also suggest Ye-ji acting out of self-interest when she makes sure her cameraman is catching every uncomfortable revelation. But all that is possibly unconscious behavior. Ye-ji’s overtures of friendship to uneducated Mi-ok seem genuine, as does Sang-woo’s generosity when he insists on taking the family out to a Korean barbecue joint for dinner, where the wives get drunk and messy on soju. Later, Sang-woo agrees to Ye-ji’s wish to invite them to their swanky coastal vacation home with its own private beach, only half joking when he calls his wife’s displays of empathy “method acting.” The documentarian obviously knows that the meatiest stuff will come from interviewing Ho-soek, and since her request of Mi-ok to nudge her husband to participate has yielded nothing, it’s not hard to discern an ulterior motive in her idea of a cozy weekend together. But sexual tensions, increasingly unignorable class distances and a shattering full-scale anxiety attack on camera cast a pall over the getaway. Leaning into his literary roots as a fiction writer, Lee makes eloquent use of flashbacks to color in the details of Ho-seok and Mi-ok’s history, from the sweet awkwardness of their first encounter as teenagers to his romantic refusal to accept her decision years later to end their relationship. Lee’s storytelling is so unfalteringly naturalistic — free of sentiment or melodrama — that even a potentially hokey scene in which Ho-seok, in military-service uniform, goes full Officer and a Gentleman , sweeping in to “rescue” Mi-ok from the Seoul sweatshop where she worked as a young woman, has integrity. There are also lovely depictions of the optimism, solidarity and hope of the early days of the strike at Ho-seok’s workplace, when the presence of wives and children on the labor-dispute frontlines fostered a real sense of community, not to mention the rare feeling for some of the women of being on equal footing with their husbands. The novelistic feel of those interludes makes the late swerve into unflinching docudrama hit even harder when we get a full account of the violence that ended the strike. Reuniting with Lee after Peppermint Candy and Oasis , Sul is devastating as the sad-eyed Ho-seok, whose closed-off nature initially seems like the sorrow of so many ordinary men whose identities are inextricably linked to their roles as workers and breadwinners. The pain of his inability to speak about the tangle of anger and shame gnawing at him is palpable. But it cuts even deeper when we witness the brutality visited upon this man who has spent a lifetime priding himself on his masculine physicality, eventually releasing his bottled-up trauma in a raw howl of anguish. The wonderful Jeon — unforgettable in the role that earned her the best actress award at Cannes in Lee’s transcendent grief drama, Secret Sunshine — is equally moving as Mi-ok. She happily chatters away, desperately trying to keep it together while her husband crumbles, never fully masking the wave of sadness that has flattened their lives. There’s something ineffably touching about the effect on Mi-ok of being around the wealthy couple. Perhaps it’s covetousness, but it seems a more innocent fascination, even in the sexual tension of her time alone with Sang-woo. Young actor Jung is also terrific, as a boy who perhaps understands more than his parents give him credit for, something hinted at in a closing reveal. In a variation on her character from Parasite , Cho deftly underplays Yi-je’s insensitivity as another woman projecting a blithe lack of awareness of her privilege. Similarly, Zo — seen recently as the monster hunter in Na Hong-jin’s delirious sci-fi action epic, Hope — stays for most of the running time just the right side of smug entitlement. As always with Lee, the movie is impeccably crafted. Cinematographer Kim Ji-yong’s camera never intrudes, lending grace and honesty to the character studies, while Jung Jae-il’s ravishing piano and string score heightens the emotions without becoming manipulative. In its scenes of factories, union gatherings and ex-employee counseling groups, Possible Love at times seems to sit somewhere near the process-based approaches of, say, Laurent Cantet or Frederick Wiseman , while its unhurried build from low-key conversation-as-action into more emotionally charged territory reminded me of Ryusuke Hamaguchi’s recent All of a Sudden . But comparisons aside, this is unmistakably a Lee Chang-dong film, its aching humanism reflecting the co-existence of despair and hope. https://www.politico.eu/article/poland-r.text: A Russian Mi-8 helicopter briefly violated Polish airspace near the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad on Wednesday, prompting Warsaw to scramble its fighter jets. The Operational Command of Poland’s Armed Forces said in a statement on X that the helicopter had entered Polish airspace at 11:08 a.m. from Kaliningrad in the country’s north, remaining there for 42 seconds. “The flight of the machine was observed by the radio-location systems” of Poland’s military, the command said in a statement, adding that ground forces remained on standby. “The nature of the incident indicates that Russia is once again testing the readiness of our air defense.” Advertisement Advertisement The incident comes as Polish prosecutors revealed that a Russian Gerbera 2 drone found in the Baltic Sea last week had been carrying a high-explosive fragmentation warhead. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk warned Sept. 17 that Russia could launch drone or missile strikes against countries that support Ukraine, and try to pass them off as accidents. European officials have accused Moscow multiple times this year of using sabotage, cyberattacks, espionage and drone operations to pressure Kyiv’s backers as Russia continues its grinding full-scale war on its neighbor. In August, Germany blamed Russia for an attempted explosive-drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport, while earlier this month Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen accused a Russian frigate of firing two flares at a Danish military helicopter. She called the incident an attempt to test NATO and said it was part of Russia’s increasingly aggressive strategy of hybrid warfare. Russian President Vladimir Putin has said Moscow doesn’t plan to attack NATO countries, but Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov has warned that any European attack on Russia would trigger a different — and “very short” — war. Tusk’s office and the Russian Embassy in Warsaw did not immediately respond to POLITICO’s request for comment.

https://www.durangoherald.com/articles/a.text: Senior NATO commander warns Putin is becoming more cavalier and open to risk as Ukraine war drags on AP AP European Security Correspondent Tuesday, Sep 22, 2026 10:30 PM MT SHARE SHARE Facebook Email Copy Link A man stands at a balcony of an apartment building damaged after a Russian drone strike in Kyiv, Ukraine, on Tuesday, Sept. 22, 2026. (AP Photo/Evgeniy Maloletka) (AP Photo/Evgeniy Maloletka) TALLINN, Estonia (AP) — Russian President Vladimir Putin is becoming “increasingly cavalier, dangerous and risk accepting,” as his war in Ukraine drags on and as he seeks to divide Western allies, NATO’s deputy commander in Europe said Tuesday. Air Chief Marshal Sir John Stringer spoke to The Associated Press at a security conference in Estonia amid warnings from some European leaders that Moscow is planning to test NATO’s collective defense pact with bolder attacks that have already included sabotage and espionage. Stringer warned that NATO members need to be aware of the “febrile environment” and be careful in their response because Putin would like to provoke the alliance into an “overreaction.” Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said last week that Russia might target NATO nations with deliberate drone or missile strikes while claiming they were accidental. French President Emmanuel Macron agreed and has asked his government to prepare a plan to protect critical infrastructure against potential drone attacks and cyberattacks. Other European officials say the threat from Russia is serious but have called for calm. A British defense official, speaking on condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive security matters, said the U.K. assessment is that Putin is not seeking direct confrontation with NATO. Officials in Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania, which border Russia, also have been more cautious about the prospect of a serious escalation after years of calling on Western nations to adopt a more hawkish approach to Moscow. “Ukraine is fighting. Russia is absorbed in Ukraine. We do not observe any buildup near our borders. And from that part, I think that most would agree that the perspective of direct military attack is not correct,” Latvian President Edgars Rinkevics told a small group of reporters late Tuesday on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly in New York. The U.S. ambassador to NATO, Matthew Whitaker, dismissed any concerns that Russia may be testing the transatlantic military alliance, telling the AP following a panel discussion in Des Moines, Iowa, on Tuesday evening that “Putin does not want a conflict with NATO.” He said drone incursions into countries like Romania or Poland were largely the result of electronic warfare and unintentional but noted that hybrid activities like sabotage “are more concerning.” Whitaker also warned against “overreacting” because “that’s exactly what I think our adversaries would want or hope for.” European countries have already faced multiple incursions of Russian drones — and several missiles — as well as a campaign of covert Russian disruption which began after Putin’s invasion of Ukraine. An AP interactive map tracking that campaign shows the escalation, from 59 incidents in March 2025 to more than 210 incidents ranging from vandalism, propaganda and influence operations to arson, sabotage and cyberattacks. NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte told the AP in Iowa that Putin “knows that the United States and Europe are totally intertwined.” “We have to make sure that we are prepared, we are strong, and he knows it. And if he does anything silly, he knows our reaction will be tough,” Rutte said. Russia is already testing NATO defenses In August, German officials accused Moscow of being behind a plot at Leipzig airport where a drone with explosives was found next to a Ukrainian plane laden with jet fuel. Last month, British officials said they disrupted a Russian plot to sabotage a drone factory outside London. In August, an Estonian defense company was set on fire and a weapons storage facility in Bulgaria exploded , though neither has been publicly attributed to Russia. Many saboteurs have been recruited online by Russia’s intelligence services and some have no idea they are working for Moscow. That makes uncovering a plot challenging and attribution often difficult. When asked by the AP in May if Russia was waging a covert campaign against the West, Putin responded: “Name one proven fact.” The line between “accidental and deliberate is quite a fine one,” Stringer said, referring to incursions of drones sent off course into NATO airspace by Russian GPS jamming or other electronic countermeasures to defend against Ukrainian drone strikes. It would be possible for Russia to escalate that activity but it does not mean Moscow has decided to do so, said Stringer, NATO’s deputy supreme allied commander for Europe. While there are “a lot of different opinions as to how acute the threat is … Russia’s attitude towards negligence” and deliberately targeting NATO neighbors “is almost the same,” Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal told AP at the security conference. Both Stringer and Michal suggested the increase in covert attacks by Moscow was not because of a failure by NATO nations to stop them but as a direct consequence of Western support for Ukraine. Putin is trying to break NATO support for Ukraine, leaders say Putin, Stringer said, is “looking at a whole number of things” to try to create division between NATO allies because his campaign in Ukraine is going badly. Michal likened the Russian leader to a “rat in the corner,” who is escalating activity in Europe in an attempt to break Western support for Kyiv at a time when Moscow is under pressure. Russia’s gains on the front lines in Ukraine have been slow and at a steep cost of more than half a million dead, even as Kyiv’s deep-strike campaign targeting the country’s energy industry has caused fuel shortages in 80 of 83 Russian regions, Air Chief Marshall Sir Richard Knighton, chief of the U.K.’s defense staff, said earlier this month. Still, there’s no suggestion the Russian leader is backing away from his goals in Ukraine. Baltic leaders like Rinkevics argue that Moscow will dig even deeper now as winter is approaching, saying that attacks on infrastructure are likely to increase over the next several months and that any possibility of diplomatic progress will likely not be seen until the spring. Putin is trying to undermine NATO’s collective defense pact by testing nations with covert attacks that are hard to attribute, Michal said. But the Estonian leader said it’s currently “improbable,” that Putin will launch a conventional military attack on Europe because of the threat of a NATO response and because his forces are tied down in Ukraine. The high level of malign activity from Russia is “here to stay” until Putin changes his military goals, Michal said, adding that the best way to deter him is to “back Ukraine.” ___ Associated Press writers Farnoush Amiri at the United Nations, Hannah Fingerhut in Des Moines, Iowa, and Konstantin Toropin in Washington contributed to this report. https://blueprint.ng/braimah-submits-let.text: President Bola Ahmed Tinubu Spread the word The Nigerian government under the president, Bola Ahmed Tinubu’s administration, and the Serbian government have signalled a renewed determination to strengthen their longstanding relationship. The need to build stronger economic partnerships and investment opportunities came to the fore again recently when His Excellency Engr. Abasi Ogwime Braimah formally assumed his diplomatic responsibilities as Nigeria’s non-resident Ambassador Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary to the Republic of Serbia. The new envoy presented his Letters of Credence to His Excellency Mr. Aleksandar Vučić, President of the Republic of Serbia at a ceremony, held on Monday, 14 September 2026, at the Palace of Serbia in Belgrade. The event marked an important moment in the diplomatic engagement between the two countries, whose relations date back more than six decades. The new development is also coming at a time when nations are increasingly looking beyond traditional diplomatic ties. During the presentation, Ambassador Braimah, who is resident in Budapest, Hungary conveyed the warm fraternal greetings of President Tinubu, and the good people of the Federal Republic of Nigeria to President Vučić and the Government and people of Serbia. He reaffirmed Nigeria’s commitment to building on the historic bonds of friendship between the two nations while seeking to broaden and consolidate cooperation across political, economic, trade, investment, educational, and cultural sphere. The Ambassador also expressed readiness to work closely with the Serbian authorities, business community, institutions, and other relevant stakeholders to advance Nigeria-Serbia relations while identifying new opportunities for mutually beneficial cooperation. The renewed diplomatic engagement comes against a wider backdrop of evolving international partnerships, where sustained political dialogue is increasingly accompanied by efforts to promote trade, investment, education, cultural exchange, and stronger institutional cooperation. For Nigeria and Serbia, the longstanding relationship provides an established foundation upon which new areas of partnership can be developed. Greater engagement between the two countries could create opportunities for businesses, investors, educational institutions, and citizens while strengthening mutual understanding between their peoples. Basking in the euphoria of the new development, an Abuja based legal practitioner, Marshal Abubakar noted that Braimah’s presentation of credentials is more than a formal diplomatic tradition, saying it represents a fresh opportunity to build upon decades of friendship and translate that relationship into expanded cooperation and practical outcomes. “As he begins his tenure, Ambassador Braimah is expected to work toward strengthening the existing partnership while exploring new avenues through which Nigeria and Serbia can advance their respective national interests and contribute to broader international cooperation,” Abubakar said. https://bnn-news.com/bnn-in-focus/bnn-in.text: Photo: LETA/BNN collage/AI Advertisements Ainārs Šlesers’ Latvia First (LPV) is among the parties that do not have to worry about entering the 15th Saeima. In the September SKDS poll, 9.2% of surveyed Latvian citizens said they would vote for LPV. This is the third-highest result, behind the United List and Sovereign Power/Young Latvians. Equally important is the fact that LPV has candidates capable of appealing to different groups of voters. However, no matter how strong its polling numbers may be, they do not automatically translate into a place in government. LPV is heading into the election with parliamentary experience and politicians who, so to speak, “know the ropes”. Among its most prominent parliamentary initiatives during the 14th Saeima – proposals that are also included in its current election programme – are allowing people to withdraw their second-pillar pension savings; abolishing property tax on a person’s only home; introducing a reduced VAT rate not only for vegetables but also for bread, milk, meat and sausages; reducing VAT on infant formula and nappies; and introducing a 5,000-euro benefit for every newborn child, among other measures. Although these initiatives did not receive support in the Saeima, they demonstrated that LPV consistently promotes its key issues and values, including traditional family values, and is capable of maintaining a high public profile. However, if LPV becomes a governing party and wants to deliver on its promises, the ability to criticise will no longer be enough. It will have to secure majority support, agree on the order in which decisions are implemented and take into account the limits of the state budget. It should be recalled that in the 2025 Riga City Council election, LPV won 18.17% of the vote and 13 seats – more than any other list. Yet Šlesers’ party remained in opposition even in the capital. This result highlights the party’s main problem: despite strong voter support, it struggles to find partners with whom it can form a majority. Advertisements A brief look at how the party emerged Ainārs Šlesers has been involved in the creation of several political parties: the New Party (1998), Latvia’s First Party (2000), For a Good Latvia (2010), Šlesers’ Reform Party LPP/LC (2011), and United for Latvia, which Šlesers joined in 2014 and subsequently became its leader. LPV was founded on the 16th of August, 2021, at a time when Covid-19 restrictions were deeply dividing society. For Šlesers, it marked a return to politics after a break of approximately seven years. The party name was new, but its leadership brought together a number of already familiar politicians and public figures, including Linda Liepiņa, Vilis Krištopans, Edmunds Zivtiņš, Ilze Stobova and others. Advertisements Jūlija Stepaņenko and Ļubova Švecova, meanwhile, were expelled after they declined to join LPV in condemning Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Conservative values and major economic promises LPV’s political niche can be described as populist, socially conservative and business-friendly. The party contrasts entrepreneurial people and ordinary citizens with a slow and bureaucratic government and promises a rapid change of course. On the economy, LPV promises lower taxes, investment, transit development and major infrastructure projects. On social issues, it advocates Christian values and the concept of the natural family, wants Latvia to withdraw from the Istanbul Convention and seeks to enshrine the definition of family in the Constitution. Advertisements At the same time, it promises to unite residents regardless of their native language, pursue a close alliance with the United States and support Ukraine’s accession to the European Union. This combination allows LPV to appeal to several audiences: people expecting an economic breakthrough, socially conservative voters, those dissatisfied with previous governments, and voters from different language groups who place greater importance on wages, prices and the way public administration treats them. At the same time, Šlesers has faced public criticism over what critics describe as his desire to preserve the possibility of eventually resuming trade with Russia. For years, he has defended the importance of ports, railways and eastbound cargo flows to Latvia’s economy. Even after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, he has said that relations with Russia will eventually have to be rebuilt after the war and that sanctions could one day be lifted. Advertisements Critics see this as a willingness to return too quickly to a business model that made Latvia dependent on Russian cargo. Šlesers himself describes his position as a pragmatic defence of Latvia’s economic interests and has condemned Russia’s attack on Ukraine. The party’s “faces” The party’s central figure is unquestionably Ainārs Šlesers, who heads its Riga list. Support for “Šlesers’ party” is largely based on voters’ belief in his ability to deliver results, even though LPV has not yet been part of a national government where this could be put to the test. Linda Liepiņa, leader of the LPV parliamentary group in the 14th Saeima, heads the party’s Vidzeme list. She took over leadership of the LPV parliamentary group after Šlesers moved to Riga City Council. According to the Saeima’s summary of the 2026 spring session, she was among the MPs who spoke most frequently in debates, with 18 appearances. Advertisements Edmunds Zivtiņš is the number one candidate in Zemgale. As a former head of the Traffic Police, Zivtiņš gives the party a law-and-order profile. The Latgale list is headed by former Rēzekne mayor Aleksandrs Bartaševičs. In the 2025 municipal election, the joint LPV and Together for Latvia list he represented won eight of the 13 seats on the city council, and Bartaševičs was the elected councillor who received the strongest voter support. While some see him as a defender of Rēzekne’s interests, others associate him with the city’s financial crisis. Andrejs Klementjevs is also near the top of the Riga list, benefiting from name recognition dating back to his time with Harmony. Much the same can be said of Regīna Ločmele. Ainars Baštiks, number three on the Riga list, is pastor of the Matejs Baptist congregation and a former Minister for Children and Family Affairs. His candidacy serves to some extent as a guarantee of LPV’s promises to support families and Christian values. Advertisements Former Freeport of Riga chief Leonīds Loginovs, meanwhile, is running in the final, 42nd position on the Riga list. The party has named him as its candidate for transport minister. This allows LPV to argue that its promises concerning the development of ports and transit are backed by someone with experience managing the sector. In this way, the party can appeal to people working in ports, railways, transport and related businesses for whom the future of these industries is personally important. Strong polling numbers and programme promises LPV was among the leaders in opinion polls during the summer. According to SKDS data, support among all respondents stood at 10% in July, fell to 8.5% in August and rose again to 9.2% in September. Advertisements Among voters who had already decided which party to support, LPV had 16.7% backing in September, placing it third in the rankings. Meanwhile, in a September poll conducted by Latvijas Fakti in cooperation with Faktu logs, LPV was supported by 8.6% of all Latvian citizens surveyed. At the end of August, the figure was 8.3%, meaning support increased by 0.3 percentage points over the month. Among respondents who had already chosen a party, the Latvijas Fakti poll put LPV at 12.9%, in second place behind the United List at 23.8%. Another 20% of respondents had not yet decided how they would vote. LPV has an easily recognisable leader, a clear opposition message and a demonstrated ability to attract votes, as shown by the Riga election. The party offers simple and easily understood answers to complex problems: lower taxes, a lower cost of living, more jobs and less bureaucracy. Advertisements At the same time, its programme combines extensive tax cuts, a 5,000-euro benefit for every newborn child, higher healthcare spending and projects worth several billion euros. These promises help sustain voter support, but the question of where the money for all of them would come from remains unanswered. Among other measures, LPV’s election programme promises a 10% tax rate for the self-employed, corporate income and capital gains; reduced VAT on several goods and sectors; the abolition of property tax on a person’s only home; the right to withdraw second-pillar pension savings; a directly elected president; and a lower threshold for initiating referendums. The party also proposes reviewing the implementation of Rail Baltica, attracting US partners for the construction of a nuclear power plant, and investing in major road and other infrastructure projects. As noted above, some of these proposals have already appeared in the party’s parliamentary initiatives during the current Saeima term. http://www.econotimes.com/US-Pressures-A.text: US Pressures Allies to Distance From Anti-Disinformation Conference. Source: United States Department of State, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons The US State Department urged Canada and European allies to distance themselves from an anti-disinformation conference after organizers included a panel examining whether the United States poses an information manipulation threat to Europe, according to US officials and correspondence reviewed by Reuters. American diplomats contacted officials in Lithuania, Canada and France ahead of the October 7-8 conference organized by EU DisinfoLab, a Brussels-based nonprofit focused on combating disinformation. The diplomatic outreach reportedly led Canada and Lithuania, previously listed as “main supporters,” to reduce their involvement. US Ambassador to Lithuania Kara McDonald was involved in discussions with Vilnius, according to two US officials. The European Union’s External Action Service also disappeared from the conference’s supporter list, although it remains unclear whether Washington contacted the EU body. France remained listed as the event’s only main supporter. At the center of the dispute was a panel titled “USA as a FIMI threat: acknowledge, adapt, push back.” FIMI refers to “foreign information manipulation and interference.” The conference program said the discussion would examine how the United States allegedly became a FIMI threat to Europe. The panel followed a scheduled speech by an International Criminal Court judge sanctioned by the United States. The State Department declined to discuss specific diplomatic conversations but said it was unsurprising that governments would distance themselves after learning the US had been characterized as a disinformation threat. It argued that such language undermined shared objectives and should concern conference participants. Global Affairs Canada said its officials would still attend the EU DisinfoLab conference but had revised participation in several panels following changes to how events were framed. Lithuania’s Foreign Ministry confirmed it canceled its participation because parts of the program differed from the government’s official position. A French diplomat said France did not participate in designing the conference program but regularly supports civil society organizations working to counter disinformation. EU officials and EU DisinfoLab did not immediately respond to requests for comment. The Guardian first reported the State Department’s lobbying efforts surrounding the conference. https://www.politico.eu/article/the-cybe.text: The exposure was immense, with AI multiplying the risks — and yet time-tested global cybersecurity procedures appeared to be functioning. Then suddenly, it all broke down. The decision by a cybersecurity company on Wednesday to prematurely release information about a flaw in the popular PHP computer programming language left much of the web exposed to hackers, triggering a panic that brought to life months of warnings of how the AI-powered era could cause widespread damage. The flaws in PHP, discovered using AI tools through a months-long process coordinated by OpenAI, caused cyber agencies across Europe, the U.S., the U.K., Australia and Canada to post urgent warnings Wednesday. Numerous governments took websites offline as a precaution. Advertisement Advertisement While no major hacking damage was immediately apparent, the way the incident unfolded over 72 hours showed how easily cybersecurity processes can break down and the outsized consequences of cyber risks in the AI era. The man who set off the chain reaction with the early release — Chainguard’s CEO Dan Lorenc — quickly apologized in a LinkedIn post. But on Thursday, in an interview with POLITICO, Lorenc said he’d shared the information ahead of time because the flaw was already being exploited. Though others disputed that, Lorenc said he believed he’d seen enough evidence to invalidate an embargo set up to allow time to find a fix for the flaws. While he disputed that his actions would have caused problems for other defenders, Lorenc conceded that the evidential threshold in these coordinated cyber defense systems is a “grey area.” The revelation of the PHP flaw brings out into the open what cyber officials have been bracing for since the arrival of the most powerful tools of artificial intelligence, which not only can be used to discover vulnerabilities but also to exploit them at scale. The cybersecurity world’s long-established protocols helped prevent disaster scenarios, in which hackers would have successfully exploited the vulnerabilities to take control of numerous websites and access their data. But the scale and end-of-days potential of AI-driven cyber risks are now visible for the world to see. This “is what happens when AI turns up a flaw that’s been hiding for years,” said Eylam Milner, co-founder and chief technology officer at cybersecurity start-up Echo. The vulnerabilities, he added, are “about as serious as it gets for the web.” Advertisement Advertisement Origin story Understanding how this week’s emergency unfolded offers a glimpse at how companies and authorities are working to stave off attacks — and how much risk they face going forward. The origins of the incident can be traced back as far as April when leading frontier AI firm Anthropic unveiled Mythos, leading some in the cybersecurity world to worry that systems would quickly be overrun by advanced artificial intelligence, with potential for catastrophic events to ensue. But while researchers did find more flaws in computer systems in the months after Anthropic and other AI firms like OpenAI released those models, they had little impact in the real world. Even the Hugging Face incident, a widely discussed hack that saw OpenAI's autonomous AI agents go rogue during an internal security evaluation, related more to the level of control AI companies exert over their models than their power to break into systems worldwide. This photograph shows a figurine in front of the logo of the company Anthropic during a photo session in Paris on February 13, 2026. | Joel Saget/AFP via Getty Images That changed this week after researchers unveiled the vulnerability in PHP, a coding language estimated to be integrated into some 70% of the web. The process by which information about flaws is released among cybersecurity officials and affiliated companies is crucial. Through a longstanding practice known as coordinated disclosure, researchers and companies that identify flaws can find a fix and share it confidentially with agencies and others before releasing to the public, meaning they don’t hand malicious hackers the gift of a hole without a fix. In the case of the PHP flaw, that process worked well, but not perfectly. Information about the bugs started to circulate ahead of the planned release time. Then, according to the PHP Foundation, Chainguard “unilaterally broke the embargo,” which “disregarded weeks of work by many parties toward a coordinated disclosure.” PHP Foundation executive director Elizabeth Barron told POLITICO by email that while it was “disappointed” with Chainguard, it hopes to “rebuild trust with them in the future to ensure we can continue to collaborate effectively.” Advertisement Advertisement After the leak— which meant information about the bugs was in the open before the fix was ready — confusion quickly ensued, with government bodies and private companies choosing to temporarily shut down their websites rather than risk potentially damaging breaches to their data and the sites themselves. Early Thursday, Matthew Prince, the CEO of Cloudflare, an internet services company that is widely used by websites to block cyberattacks, giving it a high level of visibility over what hackers are doing, said in a post on X that it had seen “millions” of attempts to exploit the flaw. Cloudflare saw thousands in the 10 hours before the flaw was publicly announced, then tens of thousands in the 45 minutes after the announcement, hundreds of thousands within two hours, and now millions, Prince said. Amazon’s cloud division also said the flaw is “now being broadly exploited in the wild.” One senior U.S. government cyber official said that federal authorities have been overwhelmed — and not just by PHP. The same day the world was racing to address PHP, they were also dealing with bugs in node.js, a widely used JavaScript framework, Fortinet, GitHub and Oracle. “The fire department is fighting multiple fires at once,” the official said, adding: “The good news is they're all one-story structures on fire, which the fire department deals with all day, every day.” Advertisement Advertisement Matthew Prince, CEO of CloudFlare speaks during the 2026 Semafor World Economy conference in Washington, DC, on April 17, 2026. | Mandel Ngan/AFP via Getty Images More to come Dauntingly, OpenAI said there’s more on the way. “These bugs are among several significant vulnerabilities we’ve already found and are working to fix, and we expect similar findings to increase sharply in the coming months,” the company said Wednesday in a statement. Matthijs van Amelsfort, head of the Dutch cybersecurity agency, said in an interview that the job of keeping computer systems safe has been transformed by the advancement of AI. “As soon as the frontier models came out, that's exactly what we said, this will be the trend,” he said. “And actually that's happening now.” Thomas Caspers, vice president of Germany’s cyber agency BSI, concurred: “We expect that [to be] happening more and more during the coming months.” AI also ramps up the risks once the flaws are out in the open. Cyber agencies’ recommendation that organizations take their websites offline was “really a drastic measure,” Caspers said. “We wouldn't have done that a few years ago or so.” But because AI has made it quicker and easier to exploit flaws, “we had to do that,” he said. At the same time, the use of advanced AI to detect the flaws may create a new level of protection against malicious hackers looking to take advantage of them. Caspers said that though his German agency has also seen attacks, it has not seen any successful use of the flaw by hackers. “It seems a little bit more complicated than expected to exploit,” he said. Advertisement Advertisement Despite the fact that AI offers a new way to discover flaws, the work involved in keeping systems protected is more quotidian, with cyber agencies urging organizations to install the fix shared by the PHP Foundation, in a process known as patching. “There are three things that you have to do right now,” said van Amelsfort from the Dutch agency. “And that’s patch, patch, and patch.” John Sakellariadis contributed to this report.
